S01.text: Every morning, before eight, someone decides which aircraft will fly.

S02.text: That decision should rest on everything the fleet already knows.

S03.text: Health data. Technical records. Spares. Work in progress.

S04.text: Phalanx Twin brings it together — and turns it into decisions.

S05.text: The problem statement is blunt. Availability is low because maintenance is reactive — and the data that could prevent it isn't integrated.

S06.text: Audits keep finding the same thing: aircraft are lost to waiting — for parts, for repair, for a decision.

S07.text: In our fleet, one aircraft has been on the ground for eighty days, waiting for a brake chute — a consumable whose demand simply follows landings.

S08.text: Another has had its hydraulic pump removed twenty-eight times for one alarm. Every pump the shop tested came back: no fault found.

S09.text: Nearly twelve hundred alerts this season. More prediction alone would only add more.

S10.text: And any answer must be explainable, honest about time — and run fully offline.

S11.text: Phalanx Twin is a decision-support digital twin for the flight line.

S12.text: It answers four questions: what's happening, why, what happens next — and what we should do.

S17.text: Triage turns twelve hundred alerts into seven decisions.

S18.text: Versioned policies and optimisers propose orders, simulation tests them against the status quo, a person approves — and every step lands on one tamper-evident log.

S19.text: Monday, 06:00. Six of eight aircraft are mission capable.

S20.text: This season, most of the waiting came from tyres and brake chutes — demand you can predict from the flying plan.

S21.text: Today's board has seven issues — each with the evidence and the score behind it.

S22.text: TJ107. The system doesn't say replace the pump. It says stop — and shows why.

S23.text: In the twin, the alarm's reporter and its suspects light up where they sit in the aircraft.

S24.text: It stayed with this aircraft through ten different pumps. The evidence follows the tail — not the part.

S26.text: So it recommends the test that resolves the most uncertainty per man-hour.

S27.text: Every recommendation comes from a rule you can read. Hard limits live in code; anything airworthiness-sensitive waits for a human signature.

S28.text: Before it reaches the board, each order is tested on paired simulations of the same futures — our plan against the status quo.

S30.text: At 07:45 the board freezes. At 08:00, orders go out — each one cited, signed where it must be, and safe to retry.

S31.text: Ask why any order was issued, and the chain answers — from data release to signature.

L1.text: All of this runs live on IBM LinuxONE: the simulator, models, rules, daily loop and audit log — on one mainframe-class server.

L2.text: Rebuilt there, it reproduces every record, row for row — and simulates a day for all eight aircraft in three and a half seconds.

L3.text: IBM Z is built for exactly this: availability, hardware-protected keys, confidential computing and AI on the chip — real-time AI for critical decisions.

S34.text: On thirty paired simulations, the TJ107 decision adds twenty-two points of mission-capable time next month — and saves a hundred and sixteen man-hours.

S35.text: Phalanx Twin. One state. One loop. One log.
